claim: SCCmec is a mobile genomic island that confers methicillin resistance to Staphylococcus aureus, creating MRSA strains.
source: SCCmec is a variant of SCC that carries a methicillin resistance gene, mecA.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction and is supported by the citation context of the manuscript.

claim: CCPol is an active A-family DNA polymerase.
source: The first of these proteins, CCPol, is an active A-family DNA polymerase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing polymerase activity in primer extension assays (Figure 4).

claim: MP binds tightly to CCPol and confers upon it the ability to synthesize DNA primers de novo.
source: The middle protein, MP, binds tightly to CCPol and confers upon it the ability to synthesize DNA primers de novo.
evidence: This is supported by co-purification experiments (Figure 2) and primase assays showing de novo DNA synthesis only in the presence of MP (Figure 6).

claim: The CCPol-MP complex is a unique primase-polymerase enzyme unrelated to either known primase family.
source: The CCPol-MP complex is therefore a unique primase-polymerase enzyme unrelated to either known primase family.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis showing no homology to DnaG-like or AEP primase families, combined with experimental demonstration of primase activity.

claim: Cch2 is a 3'-to-5' helicase.
source: The third protein, Cch2, is a 3'-to-5' helicase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by helicase assays showing preferential unwinding of substrates with 3' overhangs (Figure 3e).

claim: Cch2 binds specifically to a dsDNA sequence downstream of its gene.
source: Cch2 additionally binds specifically to a dsDNA sequence downstream of its gene that is also a preferred initiation site for priming by CCPol-MP.
evidence: This is shown by EMSA experiments demonstrating specific binding to the intergenic region containing direct repeats (Figure 3b-d).

claim: The dsDNA sequence that Cch2 binds to is a preferred initiation site for priming by CCPol-MP.
source: Cch2 additionally binds specifically to a dsDNA sequence downstream of its gene that is also a preferred initiation site for priming by CCPol-MP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by priming assays showing efficient priming on templates representing the origin of replication sequence (Figure 8d-e).

claim: The three proteins constitute a functional replication module for SCCmec.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that this is a functional replication module for SCCmec.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined biochemical activities of the three proteins and their functional interactions.

claim: MRSA strains have acquired resistance to β-lactam antibiotics mainly through horizontal gene transfer of SCCmec.
source: MRSA strains have acquired resistance to β-lactam antibiotics (including methicillin) mainly through horizontal gene transfer of a mobile genomic island called staphylococcal cassette chromosome (SCC) (Moellering, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Moellering, 2012.

claim: SCCmecs have been found in all known MRSA isolates.
source: SCCmecs have been found in all known MRSA isolates, highlighting the crucial role of the element in the emergence of MRSA.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the field.

claim: SCC elements have two common features: a single integration site within the S. aureus genome, and a conserved cassette chromosome recombinase (ccr) locus.
source: SCC elements show great diversity in size and gene content, with two common features: a single integration site within the S. aureus genome, and a conserved cassette chromosome recombinase (ccr) locus (Ito et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ito et al., 1999.

claim: At least 14 distinct types of SCCmec have been classified based on the features of their mecA and ccr loci.
source: To date, at least 14 distinct types of SCCmec have been classified based on the features of their mecA and ccr loci (Baig et al., 2018; International Working Group on the Classification of Staphylococcal Cassette Chromosome Elements (IWG-SCC), 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to classification studies.

claim: SCC elements have been divided into two groups (patterns 1 and 2) based on the arrangement and predicted domains of conserved ORFs in their ccr loci.
source: Recently, SCC elements have been divided into two groups based on the pattern (arrangement and predicted domains) of the conserved ORFs in their ccr loci (Figure 1; Mir-Sanchis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mir-Sanchis et al., 2016 and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Pattern 2 SCC elements encode three proteins: CCPol (a putative A-family DNA polymerase), MP (a small protein with no conserved domains), and Cch2 (a putative helicase).
source: In pattern 2, it encodes three proteins, which are the focus of this work: a putative A-family DNA polymerase CCPol, MP (a small protein with no conserved domains), and a putative helicase Cch2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pattern 1 SCC elements encode a small single-stranded DNA-binding protein LP1413 and a helicase Cch that shows similarities to the archaeal/eukaryotic MCM replicative helicase.
source: In pattern 1, the operon encodes a small single-stranded DNA-binding protein, LP1413, and a different helicase, Cch, that shows close similarities to the archaeal/eukaryotic MCM replicative helicase (Mir-Sanchis et al., 2016; Mir-Sanchis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by Mir-Sanchis et al.

claim: CcrA, CcrB (pattern 1) and CcrC (pattern 2) are site-specific recombinases that excise SCC from the host and integrate it into the recipient genome.
source: Central to both patterns are the site-specific recombinases - CcrA and CcrB (pattern 1) or CcrC (pattern 2) - that excise SCC from the host and integrate it into the recipient genome (Ito et al., 1999; Misiura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ito et al., 1999 and Misiura et al., 2013.

claim: Both SCC patterns encode three small ORFs containing domains of unknown function (DUFs) 950, 960, and 1643.
source: Additionally, both patterns encode three small ORFs (not shown in Figure 1) containing domains of unknown function (DUFs) 950, 960, and 1643.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about SCC element composition.

claim: DUF950 has been renamed SaUGI and acts as a staphylococcal uracil-DNA glycosylase inhibitor.
source: The first has been renamed SaUGI, as it acts as a staphylococcal uracil-DNA glycosylase inhibitor, and we propose that it could protect newly synthesised SCC DNA from host UDGases as seen in phage replication (Serrano-Heras et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Serrano-Heras et al., 2008 and Wang et al., 2014.

claim: SaUGI could protect newly synthesised SCC DNA from host UDGases as seen in phage replication.
source: The first has been renamed SaUGI, as it acts as a staphylococcal uracil-DNA glycosylase inhibitor, and we propose that it could protect newly synthesised SCC DNA from host UDGases as seen in phage replication (Serrano-Heras et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a proposal based on analogy to phage replication mechanisms.

claim: The presence of proteins consistent with replication led to the idea that SCCs might replicate after excision.
source: The presence of a repertoire of proteins consistent with replication (replicative helicase, ssDNA-binding protein, putative polymerase, and SaUGI) led to the idea that SCCs might replicate after excision (Mir-Sanchis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of replication-associated proteins, supported by citation.

claim: SCC replication could increase the copy number of the element upon excision, assuring its stable inheritance and more efficient transfer to a new host strain.
source: Replication could increase the copy number of the element upon excision therefore assuring its stable inheritance as well as more efficient transfer to a new host strain.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential function of replication.

claim: SCC replication could increase the copy number of cargo genes when under selective pressure.
source: It could also increase the copy number of cargo genes when under selective pressure (Gallagher et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation to Gallagher et al., 2017.

claim: Cch and Cch2 belong to different families of helicases.
source: Cch and Cch2 belong to different families of helicases; each is predicted to be a distant homologue of a different self-loading replication initiator (Rep) helicase from unrelated staphylococcal genomic elements, the Staphylococcal Pathogenicity Islands (SaPIs) (Mir-Sanchis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and prediction, supported by citation.

claim: Cch contains DUF927 and is related to SaPIBovI Rep helicase.
source: Cch, containing DUF927, is related to SaPIBovI Rep helicase while Cch2 contains a Primase_Cterm domain similar to that of SaPI5 Rep, which is also found in many virus and plasmid primase-helicase fusion proteins (these are often also annotated as containing a D5_N domain, referring to the N-terminal portion of the helicase segment of the vaccinia virus D5 primase-helicase fusion protein) (Hutin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on domain analysis and sequence comparison, supported by citation.

claim: Cch2 contains a Primase_Cterm domain similar to that of SaPI5 Rep.
source: Cch, containing DUF927, is related to SaPIBovI Rep helicase while Cch2 contains a Primase_Cterm domain similar to that of SaPI5 Rep, which is also found in many virus and plasmid primase-helicase fusion proteins (these are often also annotated as containing a D5_N domain, referring to the N-terminal portion of the helicase segment of the vaccinia virus D5 primase-helicase fusion protein) (Hutin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on domain analysis, supported by citation.

claim: LP1413 and MP share no homology.
source: The two small proteins, LP1413 and MP share no homology; and the putative polymerase CCPol (previously named PolA for its similarity to A family polymerases) is only present in pattern 2 SCCs.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: CCPol is only present in pattern 2 SCCs.
source: The two small proteins, LP1413 and MP share no homology; and the putative polymerase CCPol (previously named PolA for its similarity to A family polymerases) is only present in pattern 2 SCCs.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of SCC patterns.

claim: Many mobile genetic elements that undergo replication encode an initiator helicase, a primase, and a recognized origin of replication.
source: Many mobile genetic elements (MGEs) that undergo replication, such as pathogenicity islands, plasmids, and viruses (including phages), encode an initiator helicase, a primase (occasionally both proteins are fused), and a recognized origin of replication.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about MGE replication systems.

claim: SaPI replication requires a Rep helicase that uses its C-terminal domain to recognize an origin of replication found directly downstream from the helicase gene.
source: SaPI replication requires a Rep helicase that uses its C-terminal domain to recognize an origin of replication, found directly downstream from the helicase gene and consisting of multiple short sequence repeats ('iterons') (Ubeda et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ubeda et al., 2007.

claim: SaPI origins of replication consist of multiple short sequence repeats called 'iterons'.
source: SaPI replication requires a Rep helicase that uses its C-terminal domain to recognize an origin of replication, found directly downstream from the helicase gene and consisting of multiple short sequence repeats ('iterons') (Ubeda et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ubeda et al., 2007.

claim: SV40 large T antigen and papilloma virus E1 protein recognize their cognate origins of replication using an N-terminal dsDNA binding domain.
source: Functionally, this is reminiscent of certain viral helicases such as SV 40 large T antigen and papilloma virus E1 protein which also recognize their cognate origins of replication but do so using an N-terminal dsDNA binding domain (Bergvall et al., 2013; Fanning and Knippers, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bergvall et al., 2013 and Fanning and Knippers, 1992.

claim: SaPIs encode a primase that plays a role in but is not essential for SaPI replication in vivo.
source: Interestingly, SaPIs also encode a primase that plays a role in but is not essential for SaPI replication in vivo (Ubeda et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ubeda et al., 2008.

claim: Known primases belong to one of two evolutionarily unrelated families: DnaG-like and archaeo-eukaryotic primases (AEPs).
source: Known primases belong to one of the two evolutionarily unrelated families: DnaG-like (bacterial primases containing conserved a TOPRIM domain Aravind et al., 1998) and archaeo-eukaryotic primases (AEPs; containing a highly derived version of the RNA recognition motif also found in certain RNA and DNA polymerases Iyer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aravind et al., 1998 and Iyer et al., 2005.

claim: DnaG-like primases contain a conserved TOPRIM domain.
source: Known primases belong to one of the two evolutionarily unrelated families: DnaG-like (bacterial primases containing conserved a TOPRIM domain Aravind et al., 1998) and archaeo-eukaryotic primases (AEPs; containing a highly derived version of the RNA recognition motif also found in certain RNA and DNA polymerases Iyer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aravind et al., 1998.

claim: AEPs contain a highly derived version of the RNA recognition motif.
source: Known primases belong to one of the two evolutionarily unrelated families: DnaG-like (bacterial primases containing conserved a TOPRIM domain Aravind et al., 1998) and archaeo-eukaryotic primases (AEPs; containing a highly derived version of the RNA recognition motif also found in certain RNA and DNA polymerases Iyer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iyer et al., 2005.

claim: Both DnaG-like and AEP primase types are employed frequently by MGEs.
source: Both primase types are employed frequently by MGEs, including elements integrated into the host genomes, with both the SaPIbov1 and SaPI5 primases belonging to the AEP family.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about MGE-encoded primases.

claim: SaPIbov1 and SaPI5 primases belong to the AEP family.
source: Both primase types are employed frequently by MGEs, including elements integrated into the host genomes, with both the SaPIbov1 and SaPI5 primases belonging to the AEP family.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about these specific primases.

claim: Most known primases synthesize short RNA primers.
source: Generally, most known primases synthesize short RNA primers with notable exceptions being human PrimPol (García-Gómez et al., 2013), a deep-sea vent phage NrS-1 PrimPol (Guo et al., 2019), or PolpTN2 from pTN2-like plasmids in Thermococcales (Gill et al., 2014), all of which prefer to synthesize DNA, and some of which make much longer products.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge with citations to exceptions.

claim: Human PrimPol prefers to synthesize DNA primers.
source: Generally, most known primases synthesize short RNA primers with notable exceptions being human PrimPol (García-Gómez et al., 2013), a deep-sea vent phage NrS-1 PrimPol (Guo et al., 2019), or PolpTN2 from pTN2-like plasmids in Thermococcales (Gill et al., 2014), all of which prefer to synthesize DNA, and some of which make much longer products.
evidence: This is supported by citation to García-Gómez et al., 2013.

claim: Deep-sea vent phage NrS-1 PrimPol prefers to synthesize DNA primers.
source: Generally, most known primases synthesize short RNA primers with notable exceptions being human PrimPol (García-Gómez et al., 2013), a deep-sea vent phage NrS-1 PrimPol (Guo et al., 2019), or PolpTN2 from pTN2-like plasmids in Thermococcales (Gill et al., 2014), all of which prefer to synthesize DNA, and some of which make much longer products.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2019.

claim: PolpTN2 from pTN2-like plasmids in Thermococcales prefers to synthesize DNA primers.
source: Generally, most known primases synthesize short RNA primers with notable exceptions being human PrimPol (García-Gómez et al., 2013), a deep-sea vent phage NrS-1 PrimPol (Guo et al., 2019), or PolpTN2 from pTN2-like plasmids in Thermococcales (Gill et al., 2014), all of which prefer to synthesize DNA, and some of which make much longer products.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gill et al., 2014.

claim: Host RNA polymerase has been co-opted to perform priming function in some instances.
source: While most often the RNA primers used for DNA replication are synthesized by specialized primases, there are instances where the host RNA polymerase has been co-opted to perform this function (Kramer et al., 1997; Zenkin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kramer et al., 1997 and Zenkin et al., 2006.

claim: All three proteins from the Cch2 operon are expressed as predicted without fusion by ribosomal frameshifting.
source: To see whether all three proteins were expressed as predicted (e.g. without fusion by ribosomal frameshifting), we cloned the whole Cch2 operon into an E. coli expression vector with the first ORF (CCPol) His6-tagged. Upon induction, we observed expression of all three proteins (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by expression and purification experiments shown in Figure 2a.

claim: All three proteins from the Cch2 operon co-eluted from nickel beads and from a size-exclusion column.
source: Furthermore, all three proteins co-eluted from nickel beads and from a size-exclusion column, suggesting that they interact with one another.
evidence: This is shown by co-purification experiments in Figure 2a.

claim: CCPol, MP, and Cch2 interact with one another in all possible pairwise combinations.
source: We observed interactions within all possible pairs (CCPol-Cch2, CCPol-MP, and MP-Cch2), with the strongest interactions between CCPol/MP and CCPol/Cch2 and the weakest interactions of tagged Cch2 with either CCPol or MP (suggesting that the N-terminal tag might interfere with the interactions).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pairwise pulldown experiments shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The strongest interactions are between CCPol/MP and CCPol/Cch2.
source: We observed interactions within all possible pairs (CCPol-Cch2, CCPol-MP, and MP-Cch2), with the strongest interactions between CCPol/MP and CCPol/Cch2 and the weakest interactions of tagged Cch2 with either CCPol or MP (suggesting that the N-terminal tag might interfere with the interactions).
evidence: This is observed in the pulldown experiments shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The N-terminal tag on Cch2 might interfere with its interactions with other proteins.
source: We observed interactions within all possible pairs (CCPol-Cch2, CCPol-MP, and MP-Cch2), with the strongest interactions between CCPol/MP and CCPol/Cch2 and the weakest interactions of tagged Cch2 with either CCPol or MP (suggesting that the N-terminal tag might interfere with the interactions).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of weaker interactions when Cch2 is tagged.

claim: Cch2 forms large multimers consistent with hexamers and dodecamers.
source: First, we investigated its oligomeric state on a blue native gel and found that it formed large multimers consistent with hexamers and dodecamers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a), similar to Cch and replicative helicases such as MCM or DnaB (Bailey et al., 2007; Miller et al., 2014; Mir-Sanchis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is shown by blue native PAGE analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The intergenic region between the cch2 and ccrC genes could act as an SCCmec origin of replication.
source: We therefore proposed that the intergenic region between the cch2 and ccrC genes could act as an SCCmec origin of replication.
evidence: This is a proposal based on analogy to SaPI origins and the presence of repeat sequences.

claim: The intergenic region between cch2 and ccrC is highly similar among different pattern 2 conserved loci.
source: This region is highly similar among different pattern 2 conserved loci and it contains indirect and direct repeats that could potentially serve as iterons (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment in Figure 3a.

claim: The intergenic region between cch2 and ccrC contains indirect and direct repeats that could potentially serve as iterons.
source: This region is highly similar among different pattern 2 conserved loci and it contains indirect and direct repeats that could potentially serve as iterons (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 3a.

claim: Purified Cch2 formed two discrete complexes with dsDNA PCR products representing the intergenic sequence.
source: Purified Cch2 formed two discrete complexes with dsDNA PCR products representing this intergenic sequence (Figure 3b, WT).
evidence: This is shown by EMSA in Figure 3b.

claim: Deletion of the inverted repeats did not affect Cch2 binding to the intergenic sequence.
source: Deletion of the inverted repeats did not affect binding (Figure 3b, -IR) while deletion of the direct repeats completely abolished it (Figure 3b, -DR).
evidence: This is shown by EMSA with deletion constructs in Figure 3b.

claim: Deletion of the direct repeats completely abolished Cch2 binding to the intergenic sequence.
source: Deletion of the inverted repeats did not affect binding (Figure 3b, -IR) while deletion of the direct repeats completely abolished it (Figure 3b, -DR).
evidence: This is shown by EMSA with deletion constructs in Figure 3b.

claim: Cch2 did not bind to random DNA sequences with similar length and GC-content unless the 23-bp direct repeat region was present.
source: Furthermore, Cch2 did not bind to random DNA sequences with length and GC-content similar to the intergenic sequence (Figure 3b, R1and R2) unless the 23-bp direct repeat region was present (Figure 3b, R1+DR and R2+DR).
evidence: This is shown by EMSA experiments in Figure 3b.

claim: The apparent Kd of Cch2 for the direct repeat-carrying duplex is between 100 and 200 nM.
source: While smearing and aggregation in the well under these conditions made quantitation somewhat subjective, binding was sequence-specific and the apparent Kd for the direct repeat-carrying duplex was between 100 and 200 nM.
evidence: This is determined from quantitative EMSA experiments shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The isolated C-terminal domain of Cch2 (residues 400–538) bound specifically to the putative origin of replication.
source: The isolated C-terminal domain of Cch2 (residues 400–538) bound specifically to the putative origin of replication (Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), suggesting that it constitutes the dsDNA-binding domain of Cch2.
evidence: This is shown by EMSA experiments in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Cch2 constitutes the dsDNA-binding domain.
source: The isolated C-terminal domain of Cch2 (residues 400–538) bound specifically to the putative origin of replication (Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), suggesting that it constitutes the dsDNA-binding domain of Cch2.
evidence: This is inferred from the specific binding activity of the isolated C-terminal domain.

claim: Cch2 most efficiently unwound substrates with an unpaired 3' overhang.
source: Cch2 most efficiently unwound the substrates with an unpaired 3' overhang, suggesting a 3'-to-5' polarity of Cch2 translocation (Figure 3e), similar to that observed for Cch and MCM helicases.
evidence: This is shown by helicase assays in Figure 3e.

claim: Cch2 translocation polarity is 3'-to-5', similar to Cch and MCM helicases.
source: Cch2 most efficiently unwound the substrates with an unpaired 3' overhang, suggesting a 3'-to-5' polarity of Cch2 translocation (Figure 3e), similar to that observed for Cch and MCM helicases.
evidence: This is inferred from substrate preference in helicase assays and comparison to known helicases.

claim: Cch2 translocation depends on the presence of hydrolysable ATP.
source: Cch2 translocation depends on the presence of hydrolysable ATP (no activity was observed with ATPɣS, AMP-PNP, or dNTPs) and of the iteron sequence AAGTG within the substrate, and requires the presence of the predicted Walker A catalytic residue K252 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by helicase assays with different nucleotide cofactors in Figure 3—figure supplement 3a.

claim: Cch2 helicase activity requires the iteron sequence AAGTG within the substrate.
source: Cch2 translocation depends on the presence of hydrolysable ATP (no activity was observed with ATPɣS, AMP-PNP, or dNTPs) and of the iteron sequence AAGTG within the substrate, and requires the presence of the predicted Walker A catalytic residue K252 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by helicase assays with and without the iteron sequence in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b.

claim: Cch2 helicase activity requires the predicted Walker A catalytic residue K252.
source: Cch2 translocation depends on the presence of hydrolysable ATP (no activity was observed with ATPɣS, AMP-PNP, or dNTPs) and of the iteron sequence AAGTG within the substrate, and requires the presence of the predicted Walker A catalytic residue K252 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by helicase assays with wild-type and K252E mutant Cch2 in Figure 3—figure supplement 3c.

claim: MP overexpressed in E. coli was poorly soluble.
source: In our hands, MP overexpressed in E. coli was poorly soluble, but when co-expressed with CCPol the two proteins formed a tight, soluble complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b and c).
evidence: This is an observation from protein expression experiments.

claim: When co-expressed with CCPol, MP formed a tight, soluble complex.
source: In our hands, MP overexpressed in E. coli was poorly soluble, but when co-expressed with CCPol the two proteins formed a tight, soluble complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b and c).
evidence: This is shown by blue native PAGE and size exclusion chromatography in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b and c.

claim: Both CCPol-MP and CCPol showed efficient extension of DNA primers in the presence of dNTPs.
source: In the presence of dNTPs, both CCPol-MP and CCPol showed efficient extension of DNA (Figure 4a, lanes 4 and 10) and RNA primers (lanes 2 and 8), while neither extended primers efficiently in the presence of NTPs (lanes 1, 3, 7, and 9).
evidence: This is shown by primer extension assays in Figure 4a.

claim: Both CCPol-MP and CCPol showed efficient extension of RNA primers in the presence of dNTPs.
source: In the presence of dNTPs, both CCPol-MP and CCPol showed efficient extension of DNA (Figure 4a, lanes 4 and 10) and RNA primers (lanes 2 and 8), while neither extended primers efficiently in the presence of NTPs (lanes 1, 3, 7, and 9).
evidence: This is shown by primer extension assays in Figure 4a.

claim: Neither CCPol-MP nor CCPol extended primers efficiently in the presence of NTPs.
source: In the presence of dNTPs, both CCPol-MP and CCPol showed efficient extension of DNA (Figure 4a, lanes 4 and 10) and RNA primers (lanes 2 and 8), while neither extended primers efficiently in the presence of NTPs (lanes 1, 3, 7, and 9).
evidence: This is shown by primer extension assays in Figure 4a.

claim: The observed primer extension by CCPol-MP and CCPol was template-dependent.
source: The observed primer extension was template-dependent (lanes 5, 6, 11, and 12).
evidence: This is shown by control experiments without template in Figure 4a.

claim: CCPol consistently extended radiolabeled DNA primers in the presence of various templates, with the most prominent extension product one nt longer than the template.
source: CCPol consistently extended radiolabeled DNA primers in the presence of various templates (Figure 4b, T1–T4; sequences in Supplementary file 1 under 'primer extension assays'), with the most prominent extension product one nt longer than the template, similarly to other PolA-family polymerases such as T7 or Taq.
evidence: This is shown by primer extension assays in Figure 4b.

claim: CCPol-MP shows terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase activity with a strong preference for dCTP.
source: Moreover, addition of nucleotides to the 3' terminus of an oligonucleotide substrate, in other words terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase activity, could be observed in the absence of a primer, with a strong preference for dCTP, at least with this template. (Figure 4c; lanes 6 and 7 vs. 3–5).
evidence: This is shown by terminal transferase assays in Figure 4c.

claim: In the absence of MP, CCPol showed only a faint signal for a single nucleotide addition in terminal transferase assays.
source: In the absence of MP, only a faint signal for a single addition was seen.
evidence: This is shown by comparison of CCPol and CCPol-MP in terminal transferase assays in Figure 4c.

claim: CCPol has 15–22% sequence identity to other A-family polymerases.
source: In fact, NCBI annotates CCPol as carrying a 'PolA' conserved domain, and it has 15–22% sequence identity to other A-family polymerases.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: CCPol is closely related to bacterial DNA PolI enzymes but contains only the polymerase domain and completely lacks the 3'-to-5' and 5'-to-3' exonuclease domains.
source: Based on modeling servers (Yang et al., 2015) and predicted secondary structure alignments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), CCPol is closely related to bacterial DNA PolI enzymes, but contains only the polymerase domain and completely lacks the 3'-to-5' and 5'-to-3' exonuclease domains usually present in PolI enzymes.
evidence: This is based on structural modeling and sequence alignments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CCPol D169A and D324A mutants did not extend a radiolabeled DNA primer.
source: Based on predicted secondary structure alignments of CCPol and other PolA-family polymerases (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we mutated two residues within the CCpol-MP complex, CCPol D169 and D324, that are predicted to bind catalytic Mg++ ions. Neither mutant extended a radiolabeled DNA primer (Figure 4d), confirming that the fundamental mechanism of DNA synthesis by CCPol is consistent with that of other PolA family members.
evidence: This is shown by primer extension assays with mutant proteins in Figure 4d.

claim: CCPol D169 and D324 are predicted to bind catalytic Mg++ ions.
source: Based on predicted secondary structure alignments of CCPol and other PolA-family polymerases (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we mutated two residues within the CCpol-MP complex, CCPol D169 and D324, that are predicted to bind catalytic Mg++ ions.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignments with known polymerases shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The fundamental mechanism of DNA synthesis by CCPol is consistent with that of other PolA family members.
source: Neither mutant extended a radiolabeled DNA primer (Figure 4d), confirming that the fundamental mechanism of DNA synthesis by CCPol is consistent with that of other PolA family members.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for conserved catalytic residues.

claim: CCPol-MP bound tightly but without sequence preference to ssDNA.
source: CCPol-MP bound tightly but without sequence preference to ssDNA and bound much more weakly to dsDNA: when fit to a simple binding model the apparent Kd was 15–22 nM for three different ssDNA sequences, and ~120 nM for dsDNA (Figure 5a and c, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a) (for these calculations, Bmax was fixed at 100% to lower the number of variables).
evidence: This is shown by EMSA experiments in Figure 5a, c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: CCPol-MP bound much more weakly to dsDNA than to ssDNA.
source: CCPol-MP bound tightly but without sequence preference to ssDNA and bound much more weakly to dsDNA: when fit to a simple binding model the apparent Kd was 15–22 nM for three different ssDNA sequences, and ~120 nM for dsDNA (Figure 5a and c, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a) (for these calculations, Bmax was fixed at 100% to lower the number of variables).
evidence: This is shown by EMSA experiments in Figure 5a, c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The apparent Kd of CCPol-MP for ssDNA was 15–22 nM for three different sequences.
source: CCPol-MP bound tightly but without sequence preference to ssDNA and bound much more weakly to dsDNA: when fit to a simple binding model the apparent Kd was 15–22 nM for three different ssDNA sequences, and ~120 nM for dsDNA (Figure 5a and c, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a) (for these calculations, Bmax was fixed at 100% to lower the number of variables).
evidence: This is determined from quantitative EMSA experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The apparent Kd of CCPol-MP for dsDNA was ~120 nM.
source: CCPol-MP bound tightly but without sequence preference to ssDNA and bound much more weakly to dsDNA: when fit to a simple binding model the apparent Kd was 15–22 nM for three different ssDNA sequences, and ~120 nM for dsDNA (Figure 5a and c, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a) (for these calculations, Bmax was fixed at 100% to lower the number of variables).
evidence: This is determined from quantitative EMSA experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Pol active site was not required for ssDNA binding by CCPol-MP.
source: Interestingly, while the Pol active site was not required for ssDNA binding, MP was critical (Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is shown by EMSA with the D324A mutant in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: MP was critical for ssDNA binding by CCPol-MP.
source: Interestingly, while the Pol active site was not required for ssDNA binding, MP was critical (Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is shown by comparison of CCPol-MP and CCPol alone in EMSA experiments in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: CCPol-MP binding to ssDNA might be partially cooperative with a Hill coefficient of 1.6 +/- 0.15.
source: Two shifted bands were seen with these 30-nt substrates, and slight but systematic deviations from the fitted curves imply possible cooperativity. As all four experiments involving CCPol-MP and ssDNA yielded similar binding curves, we combined them to fit a Hill coefficient. This analysis gave Bmax = 88.6 +/- 2.3, Kd = 14.0 +/- 1.0, and h = 1.6 +/- 0.15, suggesting that binding might be partially cooperative.
evidence: This is determined from quantitative analysis of EMSA data.

claim: Each CCPol-MP complex occludes approximately 15 nt of ssDNA.
source: Finally, the pattern of shifted bands seen upon binding to a series of oligonucleotides of increasing length suggests that each CCPol-MP complex occludes approximately 15 nt (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of shifted bands in EMSA with different length oligonucleotides shown in Figure 5d.

claim: CCPol-MP can synthesize DNA de novo and therefore acts as a DNA primase.
source: A slower migrating product could be detected for CCPol-MP both in the presence and absence of a primer (Figure 6a, lanes 3 and 5). Both observed products could be denatured by heat (lanes 4 and 6), showing that they are in fact forming a DNA duplex and are not a result of template extension (which is in principle blocked by the presence of a 3'dideoxynucleotide). This indicates that CCPol-MP can synthesize DNA de novo and therefore acts as a DNA primase.
evidence: This is shown by primase assays monitoring duplex formation in Figure 6a.

claim: CCPol alone does not display primase activity.
source: Strikingly, in the case of CCPol alone duplex product could only be observed in the presence of a primer (lanes 8–11).
evidence: This is shown by primase assays in Figure 6a.

claim: The priming mechanism of CCPol-MP does not involve covalent protein-DNA interactions.
source: Furthermore, since the duplexes observed both in the presence and absence of a primer run similarly in the presence of SDS, we conclude that the priming mechanism does not involve covalent protein-DNA interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of products in SDS-containing gels.

claim: Klenow fragment of E. coli DNA polymerase I does not display primase activity.
source: As an additional control, we showed that the Klenow (exo-) fragment of E. coli DNA polymerase I, as expected, does not display primase activity (lanes 15 and 16) while it is efficient in primer extension (lanes 13 and 14).
evidence: This is shown by primase assays with Klenow as a control in Figure 6a.

claim: MP subunit of the complex contributes the ability to synthesise DNA in the absence of primers.
source: Altogether, the results suggest that CCPol-MP is an active DNA primase, and that the MP subunit of the complex contributes the ability to synthesise DNA in the absence of primers.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of CCPol-MP and CCPol alone in primase assays.

claim: CCPol-MP could only form reaction products in the presence of dNTPs when no primer was added.
source: CCPol-MP could only form reaction products in the presence of dNTPs when no primer was added (Figure 6b, lanes 5 and 6), suggesting that CCPol-MP is a dNTP-incorporating primase.
evidence: This is shown by primase assays with dNTPs vs NTPs in Figure 6b.

claim: CCPol-MP is a dNTP-incorporating primase.
source: CCPol-MP could only form reaction products in the presence of dNTPs when no primer was added (Figure 6b, lanes 5 and 6), suggesting that CCPol-MP is a dNTP-incorporating primase.
evidence: This is inferred from the nucleotide specificity in primase assays.

claim: CCPol alone was inactive in the absence of primers regardless of the nucleotides added.
source: In comparison, CCPol alone was inactive in the absence of primers regardless of the nucleotides added (lanes 9 and 10), consistent with our proposal that MP is required for priming.
evidence: This is shown by primase assays in Figure 6b.

claim: Only CCPol-MP and not CCPol alone or Klenow showed DNA synthesis in the absence of a primer on linear templates.
source: Consistent with our previous assay, only CCPol-MP and not CCPol alone or Klenow (exo-) showed DNA synthesis in the absence of a primer, while all three proteins could extend primers with varied efficiencies (Figure 6c, left panel).
evidence: This is shown by primase assays monitoring incorporation of radiolabeled dATP in Figure 6c.

claim: Priming products were observed only in the presence of CCPol-MP when ss circular DNA (phage M13) was used as a template.
source: A similar pattern was observed when ss circular DNA (phage M13) was used as a template: priming products were observed only in the presence of CCPol-MP (Figure 6c, right panel).
evidence: This is shown by primase assays with M13 template in Figure 6c.

claim: No primase activity was detected in the presence of a ss linear RNA template.
source: We were unable to detect any primase activity in the presence of a ss linear RNA template, while the matching DNA template enabled synthesis of DNA products (Figure 6d, left panel).
evidence: This is shown by primase assays with RNA vs DNA templates in Figure 6d.

claim: The RNA template supported primer extension by CCPol-MP, characterizing it as having reverse transcriptase activity.
source: At the same time, the RNA template did support primer extension, further characterizing CCPol-MP as having reverse transcriptase activity.
evidence: This is shown by primer extension assays with RNA template in Figure 6d.

claim: Efficient CCPol-MP priming activity depends on the presence of a ssDNA template.
source: Together, these results suggest that efficient CCPol-MP priming activity depends on the presence of a ssDNA template.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of activity with RNA templates and activity with DNA templates.

claim: Both CCPol-MP D169A and D324A variants were as inactive as CCPol alone in primase assays.
source: Both variants of CCPol-MP were as inactive as CCPol alone (Figure 7a), showing that primase activity, while facilitated by MP, requires the catalytic site of CCPol.
evidence: This is shown by primase assays with mutant proteins in Figure 7a.

claim: Primase activity, while facilitated by MP, requires the catalytic site of CCPol.
source: Both variants of CCPol-MP were as inactive as CCPol alone (Figure 7a), showing that primase activity, while facilitated by MP, requires the catalytic site of CCPol.
evidence: This is inferred from the inactivity of catalytic mutants in primase assays.

claim: Addition of WT CCPol to either inactive variant of CCPol-MP partially restored primase activity.
source: However, addition of the WT CCPol to either inactive variant of CCPol-MP partially restored primase activity (Figure 7a), suggesting that the subunits within the complex are in a dynamic equilibrium and can interchange, or that they can act in trans between CCPol-MP complexes.
evidence: This is shown by complementation experiments in Figure 7a.

claim: The subunits within the CCPol-MP complex are in a dynamic equilibrium and can interchange, or they can act in trans between complexes.
source: However, addition of the WT CCPol to either inactive variant of CCPol-MP partially restored primase activity (Figure 7a), suggesting that the subunits within the complex are in a dynamic equilibrium and can interchange, or that they can act in trans between CCPol-MP complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the complementation results.

claim: Both primer extension and de novo synthesis by CCPol-MP were most efficient in Mg++.
source: Unsurprisingly, as they require the same active site, both primer extension and de novo synthesis were most efficient in Mg++.
evidence: This is shown by assays with different divalent metal ions in Figure 7b and c.

claim: Ca++ supported primer extension by CCPol-MP although quite weakly at lower protein concentration.
source: Ca++ did support primer extension although quite weakly at the lower protein concentration used.
evidence: This is shown by primer extension assays with different metals in Figure 7b.

claim: No priming products were seen in Ca++.
source: Perhaps because primase activity is generally weaker than primer extension, no priming products were seen in Ca++.
evidence: This is shown by primase assays with different metals in Figure 7c.

claim: Mn++ supported both primer extension and primase activities but the products were shorter.
source: Mn++ supported both activities but the products were shorter.
evidence: This is shown by assays with different metals in Figure 7b and c.

claim: Mn++ lowers the accuracy of nucleotide choice leading to mismatched primer ends that are poor substrates for extension.
source: We speculate that Mn++ lowers the accuracy of nucleotide choice leading to mismatched primer ends that are poor substrates for extension and also cannot be edited because CCPol lacks an editing exonuclease (El-Deiry et al., 1984; Kunkel and Bebenek, 2000).
evidence: This is speculation based on known properties of Mn++ and the lack of exonuclease activity in CCPol, supported by citations.

claim: Neither Co++ nor Zn++ supported catalytic activity in primer extension or primase assays.
source: Neither Co++ nor Zn++ supported catalytic activity in either assay.
evidence: This is shown by assays with different metals in Figure 7b and c.

claim: Under the conditions used, Klenow can extend the primer to the full length of the template while CCPol-MP extension products are shorter and less abundant.
source: Direct comparison between the two polymerases shows that, under the conditions used, Klenow can extend the primer to the full length of the template while CCPol-MP extension products are shorter and less abundant, perhaps due to higher Km's for substrates and/or lower processivity, or perhaps due to an intrinsic preference for synthesizing short products (Figure 7d, left panel).
evidence: This is shown by comparison of Klenow and CCPol-MP in primer extension assays in Figure 7d.

claim: Klenow polymerase can extend primers made by CCPol-MP.
source: CCPol-MP priming reactions further incubated with Klenow (exo-) resulted in appearance of products longer than those made by CCPol-MP alone (Figure 7d, right panel), suggesting that Klenow polymerase can extend primers made by CCPol-MP.
evidence: This is shown by prime-then-extend assays in Figure 7d.

claim: The main primase starting site on a particular template is seven nt from the 3' end of the template.
source: Strikingly, Klenow extended most of the CCPol-MP-made primers to products seven nt shorter than the template, which suggests that the main primase starting site on this particular template is seven nt from the 3' end of the template (see more below).
evidence: This is inferred from the size of Klenow extension products in Figure 7d.

claim: Klenow cannot compensate for inactive CCPol in the primase assay.
source: Moreover, we supplemented the inactive variants of CCPol-MP (D169A and D324A) with Klenow (exo-) and saw no priming or extension products, suggesting that Klenow cannot compensate for inactive CCPol in this assay, and therefore that, while MP can facilitate primer synthesis by CCPol, it cannot do so for a heterologous polymerase such as Klenow.
evidence: This is shown by complementation experiments with Klenow in Figure 7d.

claim: MP can facilitate primer synthesis by CCPol but cannot do so for a heterologous polymerase such as Klenow.
source: Moreover, we supplemented the inactive variants of CCPol-MP (D169A and D324A) with Klenow (exo-) and saw no priming or extension products, suggesting that Klenow cannot compensate for inactive CCPol in this assay, and therefore that, while MP can facilitate primer synthesis by CCPol, it cannot do so for a heterologous polymerase such as Klenow.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of complementation by Klenow.

claim: CCPol-MP began DNA synthesis in different places when presented with templates of different, randomly chosen sequences.
source: When presented with templates of different, randomly chosen sequences but similar sizes, CCPol-MP began DNA synthesis in different places (or not at all), as seen in our prime-then-elongate assay (where after the priming reaction, additional unlabeled dATP is added to allow for further elongation of primers by CCPol-MP; Figure 8a).
evidence: This is shown by prime-then-elongate assays with different templates in Figure 8a.

claim: Most CCPol-MP priming start sites fell within 8–14 nt from the template 3' end.
source: Analysis of these priming start positions with respect to the 3' ends of their templates (Figure 8b) revealed that most start sites fell within 8–14 nt from the template end, with none closer than eight nt from the template end, which could suggest spatial constraints related to CCPol-MP binding.
evidence: This is shown by analysis of priming start sites in Figure 8b.

claim: No CCPol-MP priming start sites were closer than eight nt from the template 3' end.
source: Analysis of these priming start positions with respect to the 3' ends of their templates (Figure 8b) revealed that most start sites fell within 8–14 nt from the template end, with none closer than eight nt from the template end, which could suggest spatial constraints related to CCPol-MP binding.
evidence: This is shown by analysis of priming start sites in Figure 8b.

claim: CCPol-MP shows a strong preference for the first added deoxynucleotide to be a purine, in most cases opposite a template cytosine.
source: We did not find a unique consensus start sequence shared by all of the templates apart from a strong preference for the first added deoxynucleotide to be a purine (in most cases, opposite a template cytosine), but a comparison of the 39 unique priming start sites allowed for a construction of a consensus priming start sequence logo (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is shown by sequence logo analysis in Figure 8c.

claim: The consensus priming start sequence has vague but intriguing homology with the direct repeat region of the putative origin of replication.
source: This consensus sequence has vague but intriguing homology with the direct repeat region of the putative origin of replication 5' TACCACTTAAT (Figure 8c and see Figure 3a).
evidence: This is shown by comparison of the consensus sequence with the origin sequence in Figure 8c.

claim: CCPol-MP did not prime efficiently on a control 30-nt poly-dT template.
source: CCPol-MP did not prime efficiently on a control 30-nt poly-dT template, showing a faint smear of unspecific products.
evidence: This is shown by prime-then-elongate assays in Figure 8d.

claim: Replacing 8 of 30 dTs with the origin sequence 5'ACCACTTA made little difference to priming efficiency other than shifting the distribution of products.
source: Replacing 8 of the 30 dTs with the origin sequence 5'ACCACTTA (dT-ori8-dT) made little difference other than shifting the distribution of faint products closer to the predicted start site (Figure 8d), indicating the importance of the flanking sequences for efficient priming even in the presence of a favorable start site sequence.
evidence: This is shown by prime-then-elongate assays in Figure 8d.

claim: Flanking sequences are important for efficient priming even in the presence of a favorable start site sequence.
source: Replacing 8 of the 30 dTs with the origin sequence 5'ACCACTTA (dT-ori8-dT) made little difference other than shifting the distribution of faint products closer to the predicted start site (Figure 8d), indicating the importance of the flanking sequences for efficient priming even in the presence of a favorable start site sequence.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of priming on different templates.

claim: Efficient priming was observed for both top and bottom strands of a template representing the direct repeat region of the putative origin of replication.
source: On the other hand, efficient priming was observed for both top and bottom strands of a template representing the direct repeat region of the putative origin of replication (ori in Figure 8d), with multiple products seen for the bottom strand (the strand seen in Figure 8c) and mapping to the iteron seen in the start site sequence consensus (Figure 8e), confirming that this sequence is a valid CCPol-MP priming target.
evidence: This is shown by prime-then-elongate assays in Figure 8d and mapping in Figure 8e.

claim: The direct repeat region of the putative origin of replication is a valid CCPol-MP priming target.
source: On the other hand, efficient priming was observed for both top and bottom strands of a template representing the direct repeat region of the putative origin of replication (ori in Figure 8d), with multiple products seen for the bottom strand (the strand seen in Figure 8c) and mapping to the iteron seen in the start site sequence consensus (Figure 8e), confirming that this sequence is a valid CCPol-MP priming target.
evidence: This is confirmed by efficient priming on origin templates.

claim: The results suggest functional interaction between the putative initiator helicase Cch2 and the primase/polymerase CCPol-MP.
source: These results suggest functional interaction between the putative initiator helicase Cch2 and the primase/polymerase CCPol-MP.
evidence: This is inferred from the overlapping specificity for the origin sequence.

claim: CCPol and MP belong to neither the DnaG-like nor the AEP families of DNA primases.
source: The CCPol-MP complex constitutes a novel type of primase. Neither CCPol nor MP belong to either of the so-far characterized families of DNA primases: the DnaG-like or the AEP (archaeo-eukaryotic primase) families.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis showing no homology to known primase families.

claim: NCBI annotates CCPol as carrying a 'PolA' conserved domain.
source: In fact, NCBI annotates CCPol as carrying a 'PolA' conserved domain, and it has 15–22% sequence identity to other A-family polymerases.
evidence: This is stated as a fact from database annotation.

claim: A previous bioinformatic study included CCPol in a proposed new group of A-family polymerases termed the TV-Pols.
source: A previous bioinformatic study included CCPol in a proposed new group of A-family polymerases termed the TV-Pols for their occurrence in transposons and viruses (Iyer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iyer et al., 2008.

claim: It was suggested that TV-Pols might act as primases due to their genetic association with D5-family helicases.
source: Due to their genetic association with D5-family helicases, which often have an N-terminal DnaG or AEP – type primase domain, it was suggested that the TV-Pols might act as primases.
evidence: This is a previous speculation mentioned in the context of the current findings.

claim: To the authors' knowledge, none of the other members of the proposed TV-Pol family have been biochemically characterized.
source: However, MP was not mentioned, and to our knowledge, none of the other members of the proposed TV-Pol family have been biochemically characterized.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the current state of knowledge.

claim: CCPol shows a strong preference for incorporating dNTPs over NTPs.
source: Furthermore, CCPol shows a strong preference for incorporating dNTPs over NTPs, and under our assay conditions CCPol-MP exclusively uses dNTPs to synthesize primers, which is striking since only a handful of known primases uses dNTPs rather than NTPs for primer synthesis (see Introduction).
evidence: This is shown by primer extension and primase assays in Figures 4a and 6b.

claim: Under the assay conditions used, CCPol-MP exclusively uses dNTPs to synthesize primers.
source: Furthermore, CCPol shows a strong preference for incorporating dNTPs over NTPs, and under our assay conditions CCPol-MP exclusively uses dNTPs to synthesize primers, which is striking since only a handful of known primases uses dNTPs rather than NTPs for primer synthesis (see Introduction).
evidence: This is shown by primase assays in Figure 6b.

claim: The structural features governing the choice of dNTPs over NTPs by human PrimPol involve steric clashes between active site amino acids and the 2' hydroxyl of a ribose sugar.
source: The structural features governing the choice of dNTPs over NTPs by a primase have been described for the AEP-like human PrimPol, where steric clashes between active site amino acids and the 2' hydroxyl of a ribose sugar prevent incorporation of NTPs (Rechkoblit et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rechkoblit et al., 2016.

claim: CCPol conserves two residues used to discriminate against ribonucleotides by E. coli PolI: E710 (CCPol E174) and F762 (CCPol F225).
source: As CCPol is most closely related to DNA Pol I, we note that it does conserve two residues used to discriminate against ribonucleotides by E. coli PolI: E710 (our E174) and F762 (our F225).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison with E. coli Pol I.

claim: MP confers tight ssDNA binding to the CCPol-MP complex.
source: Primases must be able to grip the template strand in the absence of a primer. In agreement with this, we found that MP confers tight ssDNA binding to the CCPol-MP complex even though binding to dsDNA was much weaker in our EMSAs (Figures 5a and 6a).
evidence: This is shown by EMSA experiments in Figures 5 and 6a.

claim: Other primases utilize a second protein or domain to aid in binding the single-stranded template.
source: Other primases also utilize a second protein or domain to aid in binding the single-stranded template: DnaG and PrimPol use a zinc-binding domain whereas many AEP-family primases use a helical bundle that is sometimes fused to the catalytic module and sometimes part of a separate subunit (Geibel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about primase mechanisms, supported by citation.

claim: Accessory domains and/or subunits have been implicated in helping primase enzymes bind the initial two nucleotide triphosphates.
source: Accessory domains and/or subunits have also been implicated in helping the primase enzyme bind the initial two nucleotide triphosphates, which MP might also do.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge with speculation about MP's role.

claim: CCPol-MP might function analogously to bacteriophage T7 and N4 RNA polymerases, with MP helping to deliver the single stranded template to the PolA-type active site.
source: CCPol-MP might function in an analogous way, with MP helping to deliver the single stranded template to the PolA-type active site.
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to phage RNA polymerases.

claim: The last helix of the thumb in bacteriophage T7 and N4 RNA polymerases is shorter than in DNA Pol Is, allowing space for the triphosphate group of the first nucleotide.
source: Another feature of these RNA polymerases is that the last helix of the thumb is shorter than in DNA Pol Is, allowing space for the triphosphate group of the first nucleotide.
evidence: This is stated as a known structural feature of these polymerases.

claim: The last helix of the thumb is predicted to be shorter in CCPol than in E. coli Pol I.
source: This helix is also predicted to be shorter in CCPol (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; residues 151–156 in CCPol vs. 684–692 for E. coli Pol I).
evidence: This is based on structural predictions shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Primer synthesis by CCPol-MP frequently stopped at about 14-15nt in length in assays using low concentration of radiolabeled dATP.
source: Primer synthesis by CCPol-MP frequently stopped at about 14-15nt in length (Figures 6c and 7a,d and the shorter products in part c). These short products corresponded to assays that used a low concentration of radiolabeled dATP, which may have been limiting (further extension was observed when substantial additional dATP was added later in the reaction; Figure 8).
evidence: This is observed in multiple primase assays shown in Figures 6c, 7a, c, d.

claim: MP may act as an 'anchor' through interactions with ssDNA upstream of the priming site, providing a barrier to elongation and limiting primer length.
source: However, the roughly consistent size of the primers made in Figures 6c and 7a,d as well as the bimodal distribution of sizes in Figure 7c hints that MP acts as an 'anchor' through interactions with ssDNA upstream of the priming site, which would provide a barrier to elongation even if MP is flexibly linked to CCPol, and would limit the length of primers produced when the enzyme is in priming mode.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed primer length distribution.

claim: High dNTP concentrations may force the CCPol-MP system over a barrier to elongation, leading to longer products.
source: High dNTP concentrations may force the system over that barrier, leading to longer products.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of longer products at high dNTP concentrations.

claim: Many primases form products ranging from 5 to 10 nt with a particular ability to count the exact length of a primer made.
source: Many other primases form products ranging from 5 to 10 nt, with a particular ability of most primases to count the exact length of a primer made (reviewed in Frick and Richardson, 2001; Kuchta and Stengel, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about primases, supported by citations to reviews.

claim: For human PrimPol, there is a proposed conformational change between the priming and elongation modes.
source: For some primases, for example the human PrimPol, there is a proposed conformational change between the priming and elongation modes (Bell, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bell, 2019.

claim: CCPol-MP utilizes specific priming start sites.
source: The elongation products that we observed suggested that CCPol-MP utilizes specific priming start sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of priming products shown in Figure 8.

claim: Most primases do not start primer synthesis on a template at random but rather choose a specific site.
source: Most primases do not start primer synthesis on a template at random but rather choose a specific site, with the level of specificity ranging from a simple requirement for a template pyrimidine (human primase) to a short (2–5 nt) specific template sequence (T4, T7 primases) (Kuchta and Stengel, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about primases, supported by citation.

claim: CCPol-MP starts primer synthesis at discrete positions, with the first nucleotide added most often being a dGTP opposite to template dCTP.
source: CCPol-MP appears to start the primer synthesis at discrete positions, with the first nucleotide added most often being a dGTP (opposite to the template dCTP) and with 90% of the template start sites being a pyrimidine (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is shown by sequence logo analysis in Figure 8c.

claim: 90% of CCPol-MP template start sites are a pyrimidine.
source: CCPol-MP appears to start the primer synthesis at discrete positions, with the first nucleotide added most often being a dGTP (opposite to the template dCTP) and with 90% of the template start sites being a pyrimidine (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is shown by sequence logo analysis in Figure 8c.

claim: T7 RNAP shows a similar bias towards using GTP as a first nucleotide incorporated, which could be explained by the architecture of the RNAP active site.
source: It is worth noting that T7 RNAP shows a similar bias towards using GTP as a first nucleotide incorporated, which could be explained by the architecture of the RNAP active site (Chamberlin and Ring, 1973; Kennedy et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chamberlin and Ring, 1973 and Kennedy et al., 2007.

claim: CCPol-MP priming requires at least seven nt at the 3' end of the template, potentially due to spatial constraints.
source: Finally, CCPol-MP priming requires at least seven nt at the 3'end of the template (Figure 8b), potentially due to the natures of CCPol-MP binding, MP-ssDNA binding, and resulting spatial constraints.
evidence: This is shown by analysis of priming start positions in Figure 8b.

claim: Cch2 may act as a self-loading helicase.
source: Our experiments suggest that Cch2 may act as a self-loading helicase.
evidence: This is inferred from the specific DNA binding and helicase activities.

claim: Other factors (for loading or activation) may be required for Cch2 helicase activity.
source: However, other factors (for loading or activation) may be required, as we found only three iterons in the binding site, and our helicase activity in vitro was consistently low.
evidence: This is speculation based on the low helicase activity observed.

claim: For the vaccinia virus D5 helicase-primase protein, no helicase activity could be demonstrated in vitro, suggesting that additional factors may be required.
source: It should be noted that for the founder of the D5 helicase family, from the vaccinia virus helicase-primase D5 protein, no helicase activity at all could be demonstrated in vitro, also suggesting that additional factors may be required (Hutin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hutin et al., 2016.

claim: The data presented, combined with previous studies of pattern 1 SCC element-encoded proteins, strongly suggest that SCC elements are replicative.
source: The data presented here, combined with our previous studies of pattern 1 SCC element- encoded proteins (Mir-Sanchis et al., 2016; Mir-Sanchis et al., 2018), strongly suggest that SCC elements are in fact replicative.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined biochemical characterization of replication-associated proteins, supported by citations.

claim: A Cch or Cch2 operon can be found in all SCC elements identified to date.
source: A Cch or Cch2 operon can be found in all SCC elements identified to date, further supporting an essential role of the operon in SCC maintenance.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about SCC element composition.

claim: The Cch2 operon presents the same features as the replication modules of other replicative MGEs.
source: Moreover, the Cch2 operon discussed here presents the same features as the replication modules of other replicative MGEs.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with known MGE replication systems.

claim: In nearly all DNA viruses that encode a replicative primase, a helicase domain is fused to the primase or is encoded in its vicinity.
source: For example, in nearly all DNA viruses that encode a replicative primase, a helicase domain is fused to the primase or is encoded in its vicinity (Kazlauskas et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kazlauskas et al., 2016.

claim: SaPI5 Rep contains both primase and helicase domains, with putative SaPI origin of replication directly downstream from its gene.
source: Furthermore, SaPI5 Rep, the closest homologue of Cch2, contains both primase and helicase domains, with putative SaPI origin of replication directly downstream from its gene (Mir-Sanchis et al., 2016; Ubeda et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mir-Sanchis et al., 2016 and Ubeda et al., 2007.

claim: SCC replication remains to be demonstrated in vivo.
source: SCC replication remains to be demonstrated in vivo and it is not known what naturally activates expression of these genes.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current knowledge.

claim: It is not known what naturally activates expression of SCC replication genes.
source: SCC replication remains to be demonstrated in vivo and it is not known what naturally activates expression of these genes.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current knowledge.

claim: SCC replication could increase the stability of the element by providing a copy for reinsertion after excision.
